summary: We built an autonomous 3D safe pathfinding and geological exploration system to help astronauts and rovers navigate hazardous Martian terrain. Inside Jezero Crater, steep slopes (>10°), sand ripples, and boulder fields pose severe risks of rollover, energy loss, and communication blackouts. Our prototype transforms authentic NASA Mars Trek datasets into an interactive 3D survival map powered by an A* algorithm that computes the safest, most energy-efficient extravehicular activity (EVA) route. By ensuring traversal safety while guiding exploration toward astrobiological targets like the Delta Front, this tool protects surface crews and maximizes the discovery of ancient biosignatures.
details:
Mars Invaders's Project Solution

Mars Invaders is an autonomous 3D safe pathfinding and geological exploration system designed to help astronauts and robotic rovers navigate hazardous Martian terrain by transforming real NASA planetary data into an interactive 3D survival map. The system bridges complex geospatial datasets with mission-critical operational safety, making surface exploration both secure and scientifically impactful.

How Does Our Solution Work

In Mars Invaders, the system processes raw orbital data to compute safe exploration corridors across Jezero Crater. The operational workflow is structured into key technical phases:

Geospatial Data Processing (QGIS):

We ingest authentic NASA Mars Trek Digital Elevation Models (DEM) and Orthomosaic imagery into QGIS under the planetary coordinate system ESRI:103885. This allows the system to analyze surface topography, extract exact elevation profiles, and generate raw Float32 slope matrices.

Constraint-Based Pathfinding (Python & A*):

Using Python (NumPy and Rasterio), our pathfinding engine converts slope rasters into navigable cost grids, strictly enforcing a hard safety threshold of <10° slope to prevent rover rollovers, excessive astronaut fatigue, and wheel slippage.

Interactive 3D Simulation & Telemetry (CesiumJS):

The computed ~2 km extravehicular activity (EVA) traverse from the Octavia E. Butler landing site to the Delta Front is rendered inside an interactive 3D Cesium web environment. Users can toggle hazard layers, verify direct Line-of-Sight (LoS) communication, and explore geological science waypoints along the route:

Stop 1 (Basaltic Regolith): Crater floor early volcanic history and regolith characteristics.

Stop 2 (Olivine-rich rocks): Mineralogical composition points along the traverse.

Stop 3 (Clay minerals / Smectite at the Delta Front): High-priority astrobiological targets for ancient biosignatures.

The project benefits

The system benefits mission planners, astronauts, and the wider scientific community by:

Educating users on Martian topographical hazards and surface survival constraints.

Demonstrating practical, data-driven strategies for safe extravehicular activity (EVA) routing.

Bridging the gap between multi-gigabyte NASA datasets and real-world planetary exploration planning in an interactive way.

Our goal

To make NASA’s open planetary data accessible and actionable, helping future missions prepare for severe agricultural and environmental challenges on other worlds while fostering global awareness of space exploration dynamics. Despite our detailed global modeling, the prototype focuses on regional Jezero Crater hazards and does not account for micro-scale obstacles like unmapped meter-scale boulders.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages & Libraries:

Python (with NumPy and Rasterio) → for geospatial array processing and A* pathfinding execution.

JavaScript / HTML / CSS (with CesiumJS) → for 3D web application development and telemetry rendering.

Data Sources:

NASA Mars Trek real-time datasets → for environmental and topographical data. Through NASA’s open access, we utilized HiRISE/CTX DEM mosaics to extract precise slope and elevation profiles, alongside CTX Orthomosaic imagery for high-resolution surface texturing.

Software & Tools:

QGIS 3.44 LTR → for spatial alignment, coordinate referencing (ESRI:103885), and slope matrix extraction.

Cesium ion → for 3D terrain tiling, streaming, and visualization.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

We used AI tools as a supportive engineering resource throughout the project. Specifically:

Design: When brainstorming creative user interface layouts and architectural approaches, we used AI to explore possible design patterns.

Implementation Guidance: When uncertain about how to implement specific geospatial raster processing steps or Cesium integrations, we prompted AI for coding suggestions and best practices.

Debugging Assistance: During development, AI was used to help identify, explain, and resolve scripting and data-alignment errors efficiently
